CAUCASUS.s: Кавказ • კავკასიონი • Կովկաս • Καύκασος • قفقاز • קווקז
CAUCASUS.b:
Persian cosmographers placed a mountain at the rim of the world and called it Qaf. It was made of green emerald, and the colour of the sky was its reflection. Behind it, they said, there was nothing, and the nothing went on.

Some readers moved Qaf to the Caucasus, because the names sound alike: Kūh-e Qāf, Ǧabal al-Qāf. Others left it where no map reaches. The Altai peoples tell of a similar wall, and nobody has settled which mountains are the last ones.

The photographs come from the valleys that sit closest to that edge: Khevsureti, the land of gorges, where people wore chain mail into the twentieth century; Tusheti with its stone towers, reachable by one road that closes for half the year; and the Pankisi Valley. In all three, the edge of the world is a few hours' walk uphill.

On the way, in no particular order: a church on a green knoll below Kazbek, seen once in 2006 and never quite in focus since; Dartlo; the empty towers of Chontio at the end of the valley; the pass up to Omalo, behind a flock of sheep; Shatili, through the window of a marshrutka; a guest room in Pankisi; a hammock in Udabno, on the way to David Gareja, close to the Azerbaijani border; the concrete seam that leads to Posof and on to Kars; a wall near Kutaisi that says what games my friends play.

In a roadside bar on the way to David Gareja, a Polish song from the sixties was playing, about a walk along a wild beach, a long way from any sea.

Somebody in Pankisi told me of a man who had once been taken by a djinn and kept for a few days in a cave up in the mountains. I meant to find him and missed him. Perhaps he had only been drunk. Or the edge of the world is closer than a few hours.

BELARUS.b:
A country almost without height. Its highest point is three hundred and forty-five metres, a hill one climbs without noticing. What rises is forest, birch and pine and birch again, and between the trees fields too wide for the few people who work them. Once it was called the lung of the Soviet Union. In May the air is wet and does not move.

April 1986, the fourth reactor at Chernobyl, a few kilometres south of the border. The wind turned north. Most of what fell, fell here, on the region of Gomel, on villages that were emptied and handed back to the birches. Doors stand open there, and nobody shuts them. A school that had just been finished still stands in one of those villages, and the birches have moved into the classrooms.

Entering was forbidden. The man who had organised the journey knew a teacher of physics in a small town nearby; the teacher had a son, and the son was on duty at the barrier. He lifted it for a school bus full of strangers and came along, a counter in his hand, reading out numbers, some low, some not. Back at his hut, a few kilometres outside, where it should have been safer, the numbers rose. He pointed across at a wall. Five hundred becquerel, there.

Every visit to a village began with four glasses of home-distilled spirit, poured to the brim, and a toast to love. The hosts were pleased that the guests could drink. At night there was a disco: a ring of people, arms linked, swaying in front of a ghetto blaster, all of them very drunk. The girls from Minsk who had come along to translate laughed with the guests, and at some point the faces in the ring changed. Somebody said the foreigners were taking their women. Then it was time to go to bed, quickly, in a borrowed bed in a village whose name does not stay. Breakfast was fried in fat, with beer. Afterwards the farmer's wife took a bottle of one and a half litres with her to the field.

Minsk is wide and clean, with avenues built for parades. On the Island of Tears a chapel waits for the soldiers who came back from Afghanistan in zinc, or not at all. Outside the city, at Khatyn, a bronze man carries a boy who does not wake.

North of Minsk, behind the ring road, lies Kurapaty. Pine, moss, hollows in the ground that look like nothing, like places where children play. Between 1937 and 1941 the NKVD brought people here and shot them, tens of thousands; nobody finished counting. Wooden crosses lean between the trees. Maya Kliashtornaya walked with us, an architect, born in May 1937, six months after they took her father, the poet Todar Kliashtorny. In October of that year he was shot. Her mother she saw again in 1947. At one of the hollows she stopped and spoke. Afterwards nobody could repeat what she had said, only where she had stood. There was talk of a motorway through the forest.

Since 1994 the same man. Elections take place, and he wins them.

The photographs are from May 2005. Who held the camera is no longer quite clear.

COCOONS.b:
Life begins where something is wrapped. A membrane around a cell, an atmosphere around a planet: an inside appears, and only an inside can be lived in.

The later shells are built by states, and they are built to be seen from outside. From a window of the Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest the boulevard below runs straight towards the haze, as if the city had been drawn with a ruler. In Tbilisi the Ministry of Highway Construction, finished in 1975, stacks its offices crosswise like bridges over a road that is not there; since 2007 a bank has lived in it. In Dushanbe new palaces with turrets rise behind an old Soviet star. In Kryvyi Rih the city follows a seam of iron ore for more than a hundred kilometres, so that it is long rather than large.

Kaji-Say on the southern shore of Issyk-Kul was founded in 1947 for brown coal. Uranium was then taken out of the ash of that coal, and prisoners were sent to dig. Today you look through an empty window frame at the blocks that remained, with red mountains behind them.

The hill from which one sees Marzahn was made, too. Between 1981 and 1991 the Ahrensfelder Berge served as a dump for building rubble, so that one of the largest new estates in Europe is now looked at from a heap of its own leftovers.

From outside every shell looks like the next one. Behind each window someone has hung their own curtain, collected porcelain, let pipe smoke settle in the wallpaper until the room smells of one person only. In the evening the lights go on one after another, and for a moment the façade shows who is home.

CHIȘINĂU.b:
Adam Smith wrote the words invisible hand three times in his life, no more. The first time, in a young man's essay on the history of astronomy, the hand belonged to Jupiter. The ancients needed it for whatever refused to behave: thunder, a comet, a storm in the wrong season. Later Smith lent the same hand to the market, twice, almost in passing. The economists kept it and forgot where it came from. That is how a god becomes a mechanism. Since then the market has moods, nervous in the morning, panicking by noon, in need of calming, and nobody asks who does the calming.

The first exchange was not a building. It was a doorstep in Bruges, outside the inn of a family called van der Beurse, where merchants stood in the cold and told each other what things would cost tomorrow. Above the door hung the family's coat of arms, three purses, and the purse, if you follow the word back far enough, is a Greek word for the skin pulled off an animal. Leather, a purse, a family, a square: their name is still on every house where prices are made of rumour.

In Chișinău the hand has fingers. They lay bacon on a blue scale like a sleeping animal, build towers of toilet paper and give each tower a number, stand sparkling wine next to Coca-Cola so that both look a little lost. Among clocks that no longer agree on the hour lie helmets nobody wears.

One hand sold newspapers. John Onoje, born in Sierra Leone in 1959, waited more than ten years as a refugee before Moldova let him become Moldovan, in January 2011. That same year parliament could not find a president, so he offered himself. A former head of state talked in public about the colour of his skin. Men beat him, once in a toilet beneath the street, and he went on selling newspapers. In February 2024 he died.

Perhaps that is what the hand does best. It moves things and leaves no fingerprints; you notice it only afterwards, in the price.

GORNO-BADAKHSHAN.b:
Things that cross the Panj: the bark of a dog from Afghanistan. Relatives, on Saturday mornings, to a market on an island in no man's land, back when there was one. A language, spoken on both banks in two towns called Ishkashim.

Things that do not: the names of the peaks. Karl Marx and Engels still stand above the road.

Over the Bartang at Jizev, a cabin on a cable, pulled by hand. The man who took us went first without it, to bring it back for us.

On the rock above Langar, more than six thousand ibex, deer, hunters and horsemen, each hand adding to the last, from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages. From the same slope, a few stones, thrown by a boy.

Within five minutes one morning, a greeting: Geil Gitler, with a G for each H, the way Russian has it, first from our driver, then from his cousin, who had the same name and said it differently. Some Pamiri, we were told, had suffered so much under Stalin that they believed the other one would have spared them, Aryans as they were said to be.

In a single night in 1911, a mountainside, which fell and became the dam of Lake Sarez. Seventeen cubic kilometres of water have stood behind it since.

Through the window of a Soviet Kurort near Khorugh, the wind, held back by a sheet of plastic. Kurort is a word that crossed from German into Russian. The pool was empty.

In Bulunkul, in the weather station, tea. Today it is warm, said the man. Minus ten.

BEOGRAD.b:
White city, the name says. In the Middle Ages the Latin documents called it Alba Graeca, the Greek white one; before that it was Singidunum, a Celtic name that the Romans kept.

It stands where the Sava flows into the Danube, and whoever wanted to go from one empire into the next had to pass here. It is said that the city has been fought over more than a hundred times and razed to the ground more than forty. Each time it was built again in the same place, as if the place were the point and the city only its current form.

In 1999 bombs hit the general staff building on Kneza Miloša. For years it stood open in the middle of the city, its floors visible like the pages of a cut book.

GAGAUZIA.b:
In the south of Moldova lives a people that speaks a Turkic language and prays in Orthodox churches. Where the Gagauz came from is disputed. Some say from the Seljuks, some from the Cumans, some from the steppe in general; what is certain is that in the early nineteenth century they settled in the Budjak, in villages left empty by others.

In 1994 Moldova gave them an autonomy of their own, with a governor, a parliament and the right to leave if Moldova ever became part of Romania. So far nobody has had to use that clause. It is there like a spare key in a drawer.

In Comrat, the capital, I stayed with an older woman, an independent journalist, who put up travellers on her sofa.

A rapper showed me his recording studio. He told me, with some pride, that he had already played in Turkey; Ankara looks after the Gagauz the way one looks after distant relatives. The studio was inside the parliament building. When we stepped out into the corridor for a moment, a session was under way, and for a while we stood in the parliament of an autonomy that keeps its spare key in the drawer.

TRANSNISTRIA.b:
Through a hole someone scraped into the tinted window of a bus: a country the size of a coin. Some of its coins are made of plastic.

Two bank cards stopped working in Chișinău within a minute of each other, each refusing the other's number. A country that nobody recognises was entered on what was left in the pockets. It seemed fair.

At the border the money changes its name. Behind it, Lenin still stands outside the parliament, and a company called Sheriff sells the bread, the petrol, the evening news and the football. It was Easter. The streets had been emptied, for the resurrection or for something else.

A man who rents out beds wrote that he would beat up his guest. Then he wrote it again under another name, as if a second person agreed.

The hotel on the Dniester was large, Soviet and bad. Next door, beside an empty Ferris wheel, a sports journalist poured cognac and asked whether a German magazine might need someone who knows Tiraspol.

Through the hole in the window, once more, the country the size of a coin.

SOROCA.b:
Soroca (Romanian), in Russian and Ukrainian Сороки (Soroki, "magpie"). The Moldovan town lies in historical Bessarabia, on the Dniester.

In the 12th and 13th centuries Genoese merchants crossed the river here. Within the principality of Moldavia (around 1350 to 1538) the fortress was of great military importance for the protection of the eastern border against the Tatars. Near the village of Lipnic, in the north, the Moldavian army of Stefan cel Mare defeated the Tatars of the Golden Horde under Ahmed Khan on 20 August 1470. Many of them drowned in the Dniester as they fled. Soroca was first mentioned in a document in 1499.

The name Bessarabia goes back to the Basarab, a Wallachian dynasty of princes who ruled the region in the 13th and 14th centuries, and has nothing to do with Arabia. Originally it meant only the southern third of the country, Terra Bassarabum in Latin. After Russia took over in 1812, the name was given to the whole area between the Prut and the Dniester.

Today Soroca has some 22,000 inhabitants. Many of them are Roma, which makes it their unofficial capital in Moldova. On a hill above the town, called Gypsy Hill, families built houses after the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow and the Capitol in Washington. Some are finished, some half, some are falling apart; many of the owners have died or gone abroad. One of them, a man who called himself king of the Roma, is said to have built his Capitol from the picture on a dollar note. It was the only picture he had.

The magpie (Pica pica) is a bird of the crow family. It lives in many parts of Europe and Asia and in North Africa; in Europe it likes to stay close to people. Because of its black and white feathers and long tail, anyone can recognise it.

In Germanic mythology the magpie was both a messenger of the gods and the bird of Hel, goddess of death, and so it became a bringer of mischief. As the thieving magpie it was unpopular in the Middle Ages too, as the witches' companion and the bird of the gallows. In Asia, by contrast, it is traditionally a talisman.

The Cheyenne and the Lakota tell of a time when the buffalo ate the humans. A race was to decide who would eat whom. The humans did not run themselves; four birds flew for them, and one of them was the American magpie (Pica hudsonia). The buffalo runner led the whole way. Just before the finish the magpie dropped from the sky and passed her. Since then the humans hunt the buffalo, and they never eat the magpie.

BAM.b:
In Dino Buzzati's novel, a young officer named Drogo is sent to a fortress at the edge of the desert. An enemy is expected from the north, from the Tartars. He waits. The years pass in the waiting, and the waiting becomes his life. When the enemy finally appears on the horizon, he is old and ill, and he is sent away. He dies alone in a room at an inn, facing the dark.

In 1976 Valerio Zurlini filmed the novel in Bam, in the citadel of mud brick that had stood in the Iranian desert for two thousand years and had waited, like the fortress in the book, for something to come.

On 26 December 2003 it came, from below. An earthquake destroyed the citadel and most of the city in a few seconds. Tens of thousands died. The citadel is being rebuilt brick by brick, from the same earth.

HASANKEYF.s: Κιφας, Heskîf, Hesenkêf, Hesna/Hesno, Hsenkep, Hesno d-kepo, ܚܨܢ ܟܐܦܐ
HASANKEYF.b:
For about twelve thousand years people lived in Hasankeyf, on the Tigris, in caves cut into the cliffs and later in houses of stone: Assyrians, Romans, Byzantines, Artuqids, Ayyubids, Ottomans, Kurds. A bridge of which only the piers remain once carried the road from Mesopotamia into Anatolia.

Then a dam was built downstream, at Ilısu, and the water rose. Some monuments were cut from the old town and carried on wheels to a park on the other bank. A tomb travelled two kilometres in one piece. By 2020 the rest had gone under.

The photographs show the town before the flood, and the new town that was being built on a hill to the east at the time. The flats were offered to the residents cheaply. Some of them were glad to move. Others were glad and sad at the same time, which looks the same in a photograph.

PERSIA.b:
A country of many peoples, more than any list manages to hold: Persians, Azeris, Kurds, Lurs, Baluch, Arabs, Turkmen, Gilaks, Mazandaranis, Talysh, Armenians, Assyrians, Georgians, Jews, Mandaeans, Zoroastrians, Afro-Iranians on the Gulf coast, nomads like the Qashqai and the Bakhtiari, and others whose names only their neighbours know.

The photographs were taken around 2013 on the road between Tabriz and Bam, most of them by the photographer Lena Johnson.

KURDISTAN.s: (kurdish کوردستان Kūrdistān; arabic كردستان, DMG Kurdistān; persian کردستان Kordestān; turkish Kürdistan)
KURDISTAN.b:
A nation of more than thirty million people and, for most of a century, almost no state. The few that existed were brief.

From 1923 to 1929 there was a Red Kurdistan in the Soviet Union, between Karabakh and Armenia, with Lachin as its centre and Kurmanji as its official language. In 1927, during an uprising on the slopes of Mount Ararat, a Republic of Ararat was proclaimed; by 1930 it had been crushed. In 1946, in the Iranian town of Mahabad, a Kurdish republic held out for eleven months.

Each of them was a state for the length of a breath. Today the autonomous region in northern Iraq, with its capital in Erbil, is the longest such breath so far.

KUTAISI.b:
I arrived in Kutaisi by chance and took a room in a guesthouse run by a Russian who looked like a Cyclops, and by his friendly partner. In the shop next door a man of about fifty was snorting and swaying. I did not understand the language, but I understood that it was about me, and that he had placed me in the United States, which he detested.

We agreed, with hands and broken words, that I was perhaps not capitalism itself, and he invited me home for wine. He lived a few houses away with his mother. According to him and his much younger neighbour, who joined us later, the Thieves in Law had been founded right there, and until recently murder had been ordinary. His mother got angry when he played Roger Waters and Deep Purple too loud on YouTube. The neighbour told me later that he had once driven for the US military and had lost his licence after zigzagging away from the police. The neighbour himself had failed his final exam: at the door of the lecture hall his girlfriend told him that it was over and that she had never loved him. He had to repeat the year.

Back at the guesthouse, the Cyclops wanted to show me the garden. It was dark, and his forehead was large, and I said: tomorrow. His partner smiled at me like someone who knows things one cannot imagine: no, now, go. So we went, through the cicadas and under low trees, until we reached the river, bright under the full moon. He lit a cigarette and told me that the Argo had passed here three thousand years ago, looking for the Golden Fleece.

For a moment I was not in the present. Colchis, the Argonauts searching for what does not die, next to me a Cyclops whose ancestors might have come from Pelion. I was only his excuse, an accomplice: he was not allowed to smoke in front of her. I had just stopped smoking myself. It was the best cigarette I never smoked.

UKRAJINA.b:
For a few years, in the middle of a civil war, part of this country tried to live without masters. From 1918 to 1921 the Makhnovshchina, an army of peasants and partisans around Nestor Makhno from Huliaipole, held a territory in the south-east and organised it in free communes. Red and White fought it, and in the end the Red won.

The country is the largest that lies entirely in Europe, and it has been fought over for that reason as long as there have been maps. The name of its neighbour comes from Kyivan Rus, from the city that is its own capital, which some people on the other side find hard to forgive.

The photographs were taken in villages and in Lviv, Chernivtsi, Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Odesa and Kyiv.

OGYGIA.b:
...found them inside. They lit a big fire on the barbecue, which spread all over the island, burning cedar, hemlock and thuja.

There she is: singing with her beautiful voice and weaving with the golden shuttle on the loom. Around the cave was a dense forest of poplars, alders and fragrant cypresses. Birds were sitting on the branches with their wings spread out: Hawks, owls and long-tailed terns that spent the day at sea.

And up ahead, a rich and fertile vineyard, laden with grapes, surrounded the deep cave. Four fountains in a row, one on each side, and yet each of them pours its gurgling water somewhere else. On either side, soft meadows with wild violets and wild celery...

ISSYK-KUL.s: Ysyk-Köl, Kyrgyz: Ысык-Көл, romanized: Ysyk-Köl, lit. 'warm lake', [ɯsɯk kœl]
ISSYK-KUL.b:
The warm lake, its name means, and it does not freeze, although it lies at sixteen hundred metres between mountains that are white all year. It is more than six hundred metres deep and slightly salty, and it is one of the oldest lakes on earth. In Soviet times torpedoes were tested in it, far from any sea.

On its eastern shore stands Karakol, founded in 1869 as a Russian outpost. When the explorer Przhevalsky died there, the town was given his name; it was given back its old name, then his again, then its old one. A town that cannot decide whom it belongs to.

On the southern shore lies Kadji-Say. Coal was mined there, then uranium, and when the uranium ran out sooner than planned, most of the fifteen thousand people left. Blocks of flats, a kindergarten, administrative buildings stand empty. Above the town lie the tailings, fenced in badly. Every spring the meltwater comes down from the mountains, and every spring the question is whether it will carry them into the lake.

KYRGYZSTAN.b:
Kyrk means forty. One story says the Kyrgyz descend from forty tribes; another from forty girls who came back from a journey to find their people gone and became warriors themselves. The epic Manas, which is longer than the Iliad and the Odyssey together and was carried for centuries by memory alone, holds both.

Chinese chroniclers recorded their name more than two thousand years ago. In the ninth century the Yenisei Kyrgyz ruled an empire that reached from Lake Baikal to the Tian Shan; later they were ruled by Mongols, Oirats, Qing and Russians.

The republic has existed since 31 August 1991. Three times since then its people have driven out a president. In 2010, in the south, around Osh, hundreds of people were killed in a few days, most of them Uzbeks. The country is small, and nine tenths of it are mountains.

STANS.b:
Three republics that ended up independent in the same autumn without having asked for it: Uzbekistan on 31 August 1991, Tajikistan on 9 September, Kazakhstan last of all the Soviet republics, on 16 December, when there was hardly a union left to leave.

The suffix means land, place, where one stands. Kazakhstan is the largest country without a coast. Tajikistan fought a civil war through the nineties. In Uzbekistan the cotton fields that drained the Aral Sea are still there; the sea is mostly not.

YAZD.b:
In Yazd a fire has been burning in a temple for about fifteen hundred years, it is said. It was carried from place to place when the believers had to flee, and it has never gone out.

Zoroastrianism is among the oldest of the living religions. Its god is Ahura Mazda, the wise lord, and his adversary is Angra Mainyu. One branch, long extinct, placed something above both: Zurvan, time, and in particular Zurvan Akarana, time without limit, from which light and darkness were born as twins. In the material world, the Zurvanites believed, that infinite time appears only in a finite form, as the time that passes.

Outside the city stand two hills with round walls on top, the Towers of Silence. Until a few decades ago the dead were laid out there, so that neither earth nor fire would be defiled, and the vultures took what was left of them. Today the towers are empty, and the wind goes through.

RICHAT.b:
The country is mostly sky. Underneath it, a road leaves the sea at Nouadhibou, passes a hut with a flag, runs into stone and then into sand.

Somewhere in the middle the ground forms rings, some forty kilometres across. It is called the Eye of the Sahara, or the Eye of Africa. Standing inside it, there is nothing to see but gravel; the eye only works from far away.

Terjit is a gorge with palms and warm water. Atar is a market town. In Ouadane the old town lies in ruins above the new one. There we met Saida. On the drive back she asked for German music, so the car played the Düsseldorf Düsterboys across the dunes; before that, it had been guitars from Agadez.

Chinguetti is the seventh holy city of Islam, people say, or the eighth, or the ninth; the number changes with whoever tells it. In its libraries manuscripts lie under glass, and the pages are turned with white gloves. Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata have been on UNESCO's list since 1996. The sand has not read it.

PATERNOSTER.b:
The square is named after the rosary makers who sold their beads to the pilgrims of St Paul's. Paternoster, our father, the first words of the prayer. Since 2004 the London Stock Exchange has been on the square.

In the middle stands a column of Portland stone, twenty-three metres high, with a gilded urn of flames on top. Next to it, a shepherd in bronze drives his sheep across the stone, a sculpture by Elisabeth Frink. The sheep never arrive.

The photographs show the square and the Isle of Dogs, once the houses of the dock workers, where the money is now counted that the prayer did not ask for.

SELECTED_FRAMES.s: best of • forty frames • twenty spaces
SELECTED_FRAMES.b:
Forty frames from twenty spaces, each picked twice: once by the shutter, once with a red pencil on the contact sheet.

The order changes with every visit. A frame opens large; its caption leads back to the series it came from.
